title: Chapter 15 — Of The Gravity Of The Americans, And Why It Does Not Prevent Them From Often Committing Inconsiderate Actions
paragraphs: Them from Often Committing Inconsiderate Actions

People who live in democratic countries do not care for the simple, rowdy, or coarse amusements that the common people enjoy in aristocratic communities; they find such pastimes childish or dull. Nor are they any more drawn to the intellectual and refined entertainments of the aristocratic classes. They want something productive and substantial in their pleasures; they want to mix real, tangible satisfaction with their enjoyment. In aristocratic communities the people readily surrender to outbursts of noisy, boisterous merriment, which at once drives away the memory of their hardships. The natives of democracies do not like being disturbed so violently, and they never lose sight of themselves without regret. In place of these frivolous delights they prefer quieter, more serious amusements, which resemble business and do not push business entirely out of their minds. An American, instead of going out in a spare hour to dance merrily at some public gathering place, as other men of his occupation still do over most of Europe, shuts himself up at home to drink. He thus enjoys two pleasures: he can keep thinking about his business, and he can get drunk respectably beside his own fireside.

I used to think the English were the most serious nation on earth, but I have since seen the Americans and changed my opinion. I do not mean that temperament has little to do with the character of the people of the United States, but I think their political institutions are a still more influential cause. I believe the seriousness of the Americans comes partly from their pride. In democratic countries even poor men hold a lofty idea of their personal importance. They view themselves with satisfaction and tend to suppose that others are looking at them too. In this frame of mind they guard their words and actions carefully and do not expose themselves in ways that would reveal their shortcomings; to keep their dignity, they think they must keep a grave face.

But I detect another cause, deeper and more powerful, which produces this astonishing gravity among the Americans by instinct. Under a despotism, communities sometimes give way to bursts of vehement joy, but they are generally gloomy and sullen, because they are afraid. Under absolute monarchies that the customs and mores of the country temper, people are often cheerful and even-tempered, because they have some freedom and a good deal of security and so are spared the most important cares of life. But all free peoples are serious, because their minds are habitually absorbed in contemplating some dangerous or difficult purpose. This is especially true of those free nations that form democratic communities. In them, a very large number of men in every class are constantly occupied with the serious affairs of government, and those whose thoughts are not turned to the running of the commonwealth are wholly absorbed in making a private fortune. Among such a people a serious demeanor ceases to be the trait of certain men and becomes a habit of the nation.

We are told of small democracies in antiquity whose citizens met in the public squares wearing garlands of roses and spent nearly all their time in dancing and theatrical entertainments. I no more believe in such republics than in Plato’s; or, if what we read really happened, I do not hesitate to say that these supposed democracies were made up of very different elements from ours and had nothing in common with ours except the name. But we must not suppose that, in the midst of all their toil, the people who live in democracies think themselves pitiable; the opposite is observed. No men are fonder of their own condition. Life would have no savor for them if they were freed from the anxieties that torment them, and they show more attachment to their cares than aristocratic nations show to their pleasures.

Next I am led to ask how these same democratic nations, so serious as they are, sometimes act so thoughtlessly. The Americans, who almost always keep a sober bearing and a cold air, nevertheless often let a sudden passion or a hasty opinion carry them far beyond the bounds of reason, and they sometimes commit strange absurdities with a straight face. This contrast should not surprise us. There is a kind of ignorance that arises from extreme publicity. In despotic States men do not know how to act, because they are told nothing; in democratic nations they often act at random, because nothing is left untold. The former do not know — the latter forget; and the main features of each picture are lost to them in a confusion of details.

It is astonishing what imprudent language a public man can sometimes use in free countries, and especially in democratic States, without being compromised. In absolute monarchies, by contrast, a few words let slip by accident are enough to expose him forever and ruin him beyond hope of recovery. What precedes explains this. When a man speaks in the midst of a great crowd, many of his words are not heard, or are quickly wiped from the memories of those who hear them; but in the silence of a mute and motionless throng the slightest whisper reaches the ear.

In democracies men are never stationary; a thousand chances toss them back and forth, and their lives are always at the mercy of unforeseen or, so to speak, improvised circumstances. So they are often forced to do things they have learned imperfectly, to say things they understand imperfectly, and to take up work for which a long apprenticeship has not prepared them. In aristocracies each man has a single object that he pursues without letting up, but among democratic nations a man’s existence is more complex. The same mind will almost always take in several objects at once, and these objects are often wholly unrelated to each other. Since the mind cannot know them all well, it is easily content with imperfect ideas of each.

When the inhabitant of democracies is not driven by his needs, he is at least driven by his desires, for of all the possessions he sees around him, none is wholly out of his reach. He therefore does everything in a hurry, is always satisfied with “pretty well,” and never stops for more than a moment to consider what he has done. His curiosity is at once insatiable and cheaply satisfied, for he cares more about knowing a great deal quickly than about knowing anything well; he has no time and little taste for getting to the bottom of things. So democratic peoples are grave, because their social and political condition constantly leads them into serious occupations; and they act thoughtlessly, because they give each of these occupations so little time and attention. The habit of inattention must be regarded as the greatest bane of the democratic character.
